newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German, French telecoms groups mull shr swap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German, French telecoms groups mull shr swap.

text.p: France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom, Europe's two largest telecommunications groups, are in negotiations to cement their strategic alliance with an agreement to exchange shares, Deutsche Telekom finance chief Joachim Kroeske said on Friday.
"An equity swap is very likely on the basis of decisions of the companies," he told Reuters Financial Television before leaving for talks with France Telecom."In the long term there is no doubt."

An exchange of shares would probably be a largely symbolic gesture to prove to customers that the two companies' so-called Atlas alliance was a marriage meant to last and serve as the basis for international growth.
It would also bring the two groups closer together at a time when European industry is getting ready for full competition on January 1, 1998.
The companies were once thought to be thinking of swapping a 25 percent stake in each other, but industry analysts now believe an exchange would be for less than half that size.

After opposing the France Telecom sale during the French election campaign, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said this week he was "not against" the idea but wants to consult the telecom operator's staff first.
A deal would probably need European Commission approval.

As Germany and France prepared to privatise their phone monopolies and Europe began taking steps towards opening the telecoms sector to competition, Bonn and Paris moved to link the two phone giants strategically.

The move was largely defensive, aimed at making it more difficult for rivals like British Telecom or AT&T Corp to establish a beachhead in Europe's largest and most lucrative telecommunications markets.

But the link also provided Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom with the size and capital to begin a campaign of international expansion. The first, most important step in this direction was the decision to take a joint stake of around 20 percent in Sprint Corp, the number three U.S. long-distance carrier.

The move was a reaction to the alliance of British Telecom and Sprint's U.S. rival MCI Communications and sparked the beginning of a dizzying race to form global alliances to meet the communications needs of multinational corporations.
British Telecom and MCI have now agreed to merge.

Industry analysts point out that Sprint is vulnerable to a takeover, which would seriously threaten the global plans of France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom. This in turn sparked speculation that the German and French phone companies are seeking to raise their stakes in Sprint or take it over.
But, reflecting recent denials by France Telecom, Kroeske sought to play down such speculation.
"Until now we are very happy with our 10 percent. Together (with France Telecom) we have a little more than 20 percent. So that's a very good position," said Kroeske.
"Sprint is the core activity in our whole strategy so we have to follow if there are reactions from the other side," said Kroeske.
